Heinrich Stahl
hine'rikh shtahl
n. (c. 1600–1657; superintendent in Estonia, author of the first Estonian grammar and handbook)
Stahl, a German surname from Stahl, steel; Heinrich, from Old High German heim, home, and rih, ruler.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Heinrich Stahl was born in Reval, studied at Rostock, Greifswald and Wittenberg, and served as pastor, then provost, and from 1641 superintendent of the Estonian church in Swedish Ingria and Estonia. Between 1632 and 1638 he brought out his Hand- und Hausbuch fur das Furstenthum Esthen in four parts: a catechism, the gospel and epistle readings, prayers and hymns, all in Estonian with the German facing, and a grammar of the language — the first ever written — so that German pastors could learn to preach in it. He also published a book of Estonian sermons. His Estonian is heavily Germanised and later writers criticised it hard; it was also the first usable tool any pastor had. The dictionary records him for the aim stated in his preface and in Nehemiah's Levites: to make the reading understood. “that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God” (Deu 31:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a handbook as a manual, a book for ready use; and to guide as to lead, to direct, to instruct and superintend.

expand to see more

GRAMMAR, n. [Gr. gramma, a letter.] The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a system of principles and rules for the use of a language.

MANUAL, n. [L. manualis.] A small book, such as may be carried in the hand, or conveniently handled; a handbook.

GUIDE, v.t. To lead or direct in a way; to conduct; to influence; to instruct and superintend.

ATTENDANCE, n. The act of waiting on; a giving heed to; close application.

SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.

Key Scripture

Deu 31:12 — "Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God, and observe to do all the words of this law:"

Act 8:30 — "And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?"

Act 8:31 — "And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him."

1Ti 4:13 — "Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine."

Modern Corruption

Superintendent of the Estonian church from 1641, whose Hand- und Hausbuch of 1632 to 1638 gave Estonian its first grammar, catechism and book of readings.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a scholarly judgment on Stahl that the dictionary should report and then weigh. His Estonian is bad: German word order, German idiom, a syntax no Estonian peasant would produce, and later writers from Forselius onwards had to undo much of it. That criticism is right. It is also true that before Stahl a German pastor sent to an Estonian parish had no grammar, no printed catechism and no readings, and after Stahl he had all three. A flawed instrument in hand beats a perfect one unwritten.

The principle to recover is that a hearer needs a guide and that providing one is a commanded ministry rather than a courtesy. Moses orders the whole population assembled, including the foreigner, for the purpose of comprehension: “that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God” (Deu 31:12). The Ethiopian is reading the right book and asks the honest question — “How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31) — after Philip has asked him the diagnostic one: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). Timothy is told to give attendance to reading, exhortation and doctrine in that order (1Ti 4:13).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lamad (H3925), to learn or teach; Greek hodegeo (G3594), to guide or lead the way.

expand to see more

Hebrew lamad (H3925) — to learn, to teach by repetition; Deuteronomy 31:12.

Hebrew qahal (H6950) — to assemble, to gather a congregation; Deuteronomy 31:12.

Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, to understand; “Understandest thou what thou readest?”, Acts 8:30.

Greek hodegeo (G3594) — to lead the way, to guide; Acts 8:31.

Greek anagnosis (G320) — a reading, the public reading of Scripture; 1 Timothy 4:13.

Usage

"“that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God” (Deu 31:12) — the first Estonian grammar, written for German pastors."

"“How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31) — a catechism and the readings put into Estonian, 1632 to 1638."

"“give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) — superintendent of the Estonian church from 1641."
